CausalChain: Heavy alcohol consumption -> Increased acetaldehyde and ROS production -> Gut barrier disruption and dysbiosis with loss of butyrate-producing bacteria -> Increased intestinal permeability -> LPS translocation to the liver -> Kupffer cell activation and cytokine release -> Chronic hepatic inflammation and activation of oncogenic pathways -> Development of cirrhosis and HCC; Conversely, restoration of butyrate-producing bacteria -> Improved gut barrier integrity -> Reduced LPS translocation -> Decreased hepatic inflammatory signaling -> Lower progression to HCC
Hypothesis: Enhancing butyrate-producing gut bacteria in heavy alcohol consumers can restore gut barrier function, attenuate hepatic inflammation, and thereby reduce the progression from alcohol-associated cirrhosis to hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) and its progression to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) involve a multifactorial cascade of events including alcohol metabolism, oxidative stress, gut barrier dysfunction, and immune activation. Recent evidence underscores the role of gut dysbiosis in potentiating hepatic inflammation by facilitating the translocation of endotoxins such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) into portal circulation. In this context, a novel approach based on modulating the gut microbiota is proposed. Specifically, enhancing populations of butyrate-producing bacteria to restore gut barrier integrity may decrease LPS translocation and subsequent hepatic inflammation. This integrated hypothesis suggests that targeted microbiome interventions hold promise as an adjunctive strategy to reduce the risk of HCC in alcohol-induced cirrhosis.
